What Is Win-Loss Analysis?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 9 June 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

Win-loss analysis is the structured study of why deals are won or lost, based mainly on interviews with the buyers who made the decision. It compares what buyers say with what the CRM recorded, finds patterns across deals, and feeds them back into positioning, sales process, pricing and product. Done well, it turns closed deals from outcomes into evidence.

What win-loss analysis means

Every CRM records whether a deal was won or lost. Few record why with any reliability. Win-loss analysis fills that gap by going to the source: the buyer.

A programme has three parts. First, it collects evidence from buyers after a decision, usually in a 20- to 30-minute interview, sometimes supplemented by a short survey. Second, it codes the answers into themes and compares them with seller-recorded reasons and deal data. Third, it routes the findings to the people who can act: marketing for positioning, sales leadership for process, product for the roadmap, and finance for pricing.

Win-loss analysis isWin-loss analysis is not
Buyer interviews after a decisionA seller filling in a loss reason
Wins, losses and no-decisions togetherA post-mortem on the biggest lost deal
Patterns across many dealsOne anecdote repeated in a meeting
Findings routed to owners with actionsA slide deck read once

Why it matters for a commercial team

Seller reasons are a weak signal

Sellers are asked for a loss reason at the moment they least want to give one, and they often do not know. Buyers hold internal debates and executive conversations that never reach the seller. Clozd, which sells win-loss services, reports that buyer and seller reasons align only 15% of the time, and that sellers are wrong about why deals are won and lost 60% to 85% of the time. The figures are vendor-reported without published methodology, so treat them as an indication of direction rather than a benchmark.

Many losses are not to a competitor

Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna's research, published in The JOLT Effect, analysed about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations and found that 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision. A programme that only interviews competitive losses misses the largest category. Berkowitz makes the same point: interview wins and losses, and do not ignore buyers who chose to do nothing.

Rigour is what produces the gain

The Gartner work, as summarised by Berkowitz, sets out the conditions. Interviews should be run by an independent party with no stake in the outcome. They should cover the whole decision process, because early-stage issues often surface later as closing failures. Findings should feed segmentation, sales process and product roadmap. Gartner research cited by Clozd associates rigorous, ongoing programmes with up to a 50% improvement in win rates and a 15% to 30% increase in revenue. Those are upper bounds from organisations already committed to the practice, not a typical result.

How to run a first round

A mid-size firm does not need a platform to start. It needs a short list of deals, a neutral interviewer and a fixed question set.

  1. Pick the deals. Select 12 to 20 decisions from the last two quarters: roughly equal wins, competitive losses and no-decisions. Clozd suggests themes reach saturation around 25 to 30 interviews per segment, so treat a first round as directional.
  2. Choose the interviewer. Someone who did not work the deal: an operations lead, a founder for lost deals they did not touch, or an outside firm.
  3. Ask about the decision, not the seller. What triggered the search, who was involved, what alternatives were considered, what nearly changed the outcome, and what the deciding factor was.
  4. Code against the CRM. Put the buyer's stated reason next to the recorded loss reason for each deal. The mismatch rate is your first finding.
  5. Route and record. Each theme gets an owner, an action and a review date. In lowob's terms, each becomes a decision in the record, with reason, owner, status and expected outcome.
MethodStrengthWeaknessBest for
Buyer interviewDepth, nuance, unprompted reasonsCostly, smaller sampleStrategic or high-value deals
Buyer surveyScale, trend trackingLow response, shallow answersValidating interview themes
CRM loss reasonsComplete coverage, cheapSeller bias, often wrongTriage and trend lines
Call recording reviewShows what was actually saidMisses internal buyer debateExecution and messaging gaps

lowob takeaways

  • Ask the buyer. Seller-recorded reasons are a starting point, not an answer.
  • Include no-decisions. Losses to the status quo are often the largest category.
  • Use a neutral interviewer. Independence is what makes buyers candid.
  • Route every finding to an owner. Analysis without a recorded decision changes nothing.

Common questions

What is win-loss analysis in sales?

It is the structured study of why deals are won or lost, mainly through interviews with the buyers who decided, compared against CRM records and deal data.

How many win-loss interviews do you need?

A first round of 12 to 20 gives direction. Clozd suggests themes stabilise at around 25 to 30 interviews per segment.

Who should conduct win-loss interviews?

Someone with no stake in the deal. Gartner's guidance is that an independent party produces more candid answers than the seller or their manager.

Should you interview won deals as well as lost ones?

Yes. Wins show what to repeat, and Gartner's guidance treats them as among the most instructive interviews in a programme.
